screens.body:
IoT — the Internet of Things — is everyday objects with sensors and an internet connection: thermostats, fitness bands, delivery vans, soil sensors on farms.

Each 'thing' is small and dumb on its own. The magic is the network: thousands of devices reporting data that software turns into decisions.

options: Everyday objects with sensors + internet connection
check.question: IoT means…

screens.heading: Everyday objects, online

screens.body:
One sensor is a gadget. Ten thousand sensors are a data firehose. IoT devices stream readings — temperature, location, vibration — to the cloud, where dashboards and alerts make the data useful.

Your job as a dev: receive that stream, store it sanely, and turn it into something a human can act on.

options: Receive the stream, store it, turn it into action
check.question: The dev's job in IoT:

screens.heading: The data firehose
screens.keyPoint: Sensors talk, your code listens and decides.

screens.body:
Edge computing means running the computation close to where the data is born — on the device itself or a nearby gateway — instead of sending everything to a faraway cloud.

Why? Latency. A self-driving car can't wait 200ms for a cloud round-trip to decide to brake. Neither can a factory robot stopping a jammed press.

options: Computing near the data source to cut latency
check.question: Edge computing is…

screens.heading: Compute near the source
screens.keyPoint: When milliseconds matter, don't phone home.

screens.body:
Edge and cloud aren't rivals — they're a team. Edge handles the urgent and the local (filter noise, react fast); the cloud handles the heavy and the historical (train models, long-term storage, dashboards).

Think: the thermostat decides 'turn on heat' locally in milliseconds, then sends hourly summaries to the cloud for your energy report.

options: Edge reacts fast locally; cloud analyzes long-term
check.question: How do edge and cloud split the work?

screens.heading: Edge + cloud: a team

screens.body:
A typical IoT pipeline has four stages: sense (device reads the world), send (data travels, maybe via a gateway), store (cloud database keeps history), act (dashboard alert, or a command back to the device).

Draw this pipeline for any IoT idea and you've done half the architecture work already.
screens.heading: Sense → send → store → act

screens.body:
Real examples keep it concrete: a smart thermostat learning your schedule, a delivery company tracking every van's location and fuel, a farmer's soil sensors deciding when to irrigate.

Notice the pattern: boring physical thing + sensor + your software = a product someone pays for.

options: Boring thing + sensor + software = paid product
check.question: Where does IoT show up?

screens.heading: Real examples
screens.keyPoint: Sensors make the physical world programmable.

screens.body:
IoT has a dark side: millions of devices ship with default passwords like admin/admin, never get updates, and become botnets. The 2016 Mirai attack hijacked cameras and routers this way.

Dev lesson: force password changes on setup, ship updates, and collect the minimum data you need. Security isn't optional when your code lives in people's homes.

options: Collect as much data as possible
Change defaults, ship updates, minimize data
check.question: The #1 IoT security lesson:

screens.heading: The security warning
screens.keyPoint: Default passwords built a botnet. Don't repeat it.
